Cycle and boundary subobjects of a complex
The boundary subobject factors through the cycle subobject
items.strategy: Apply d_n d_{n+1}=0. The image inclusion of d_{n+1} then equalizes d_n and 0, so the kernel universal property of Z_n(C)=ker(d_n) yields the unique factorization.

items.title: Homology object of a chain complex
Cohomology object of a cochain complex
Exactness of a complex at a degree and acyclic complexes
A complex is exact at n exactly when its nth homology is zero
items.strategy: Unpack exactness at n as the equality of B_n(C) and Z_n(C). Then use the cokernel description of H_n(C) to show that the quotient is zero exactly when the boundary inclusion is an isomorphism.

items.title: An exact sequence is a complex, and its exactness agrees with the earlier notion
items.strategy: The equation g f = 0 at each consecutive pair comes from exactness. Exactness at the middle object is then literally the same image-kernel comparison as in the published exact-sequence definition.

items.title: Chain map
Cochain map
Identities and composites of chain maps are chain maps
items.strategy: The identity squares commute trivially, and for a composite g o f the two differential comparisons concatenate to the same component map.

items.title: The category of chain complexes
A chain map carries cycles to cycles and boundaries to boundaries
items.strategy: Use the commuting differential squares twice: once to factor f_n through the kernels Z_n(C) -> Z_n(D), and once to compare f_n d_{C,n+1} with d_{D,n+1} f_{n+1} so that images factor through images.

items.title: A chain map induces a well-defined map on homology
items.strategy: Item 16 gives a morphism Z_n(C) -> Z_n(D) carrying the boundary subobject of C into that of D. The cokernel universal property of H_n then yields the unique induced arrow H_n(f).

items.title: Homology respects identities and composition
items.strategy: Both claims are uniqueness statements for the induced quotient arrow: the identity induces the unique arrow compatible with the identity on cycles, and the induced map of a composite is the unique arrow compatible with the composite on cycles.

items.title: Homology is an additive functor
items.strategy: Functoriality is item 18. Additivity follows because the sum f + g of chain maps acts on cycles and boundaries degreewise, so the induced arrow on the quotient is H_n(f) + H_n(g).

items.title: Quasi-isomorphism
Isomorphisms of complexes are quasi-isomorphisms
items.strategy: If f has a chain inverse g, then item 18 gives H_n(g) H_n(f) = 1 and H_n(f) H_n(g) = 1 for every n, so each H_n(f) is an isomorphism.

items.title: A chain map is a quasi-isomorphism exactly when its cochain reindexing is
items.strategy: Reindex C_n as C^{-n}. Under that dictionary H_n of the chain complex is the same object as H^{-n} of the cochain complex, so the homology isomorphism condition is unchanged.

items.title: Subcomplex
The differential descends to a quotient complex
items.strategy: For a subcomplex S subset C, the composite C_n -> C_{n-1} -> C_{n-1}/S_{n-1} kills S_n because the differential restricts to S. Hence the cokernel universal property gives the descended map C_n/S_n -> C_{n-1}/S_{n-1}, and d^2 = 0 survives after quotienting.

items.title: Quotient complex
Short exact sequence of complexes
The kernel of a chain map is computed degreewise
items.strategy: If f : C -> D is a chain map, the commuting squares show that d_C carries ker(f_n) into ker(f_{n-1}). These restricted differentials make the component kernels into a complex, and the universal property is checked componentwise.

items.title: The cokernel of a chain map is computed degreewise
items.strategy: Because f intertwines the differentials, d_D carries the image of f_n into the image of f_{n-1}. So each d_D descends to the component cokernel, and the universal property of the cokernel is again verified degreewise.

items.title: Images and coimages of chain maps are computed degreewise
items.strategy: Images are kernels of cokernels and coimages are cokernels of kernels. Applying items 27 and 28 degreewise identifies both constructions componentwise, and the coimage-to-image comparison is therefore the family of component comparisons.

items.title: The category of complexes in an additive category is additive
items.strategy: Add chain maps componentwise and use bilinearity of composition in the ambient additive category. The zero complex is the zero object, and binary biproducts are formed degreewise with componentwise differentials.

items.title: The category of complexes in an abelian category is abelian
items.strategy: Items 27 and 28 produce kernels and cokernels degreewise, item 29 identifies images and coimages degreewise, and item 30 gives additivity. The componentwise abelian-category axioms then show the coimage-image comparison is an isomorphism in every degree.

items.title: A sequence of chain maps is exact exactly when it is exact degreewise
items.strategy: In the abelian category of complexes from item 31, exactness is tested by image-kernel equality. Item 29 identifies those images and kernels degreewise, so exactness in Ch(A) is equivalent to exactness in each degree.

items.title: A subcomplex is the kernel of its quotient map
items.strategy: The quotient map C -> C/S has component kernel S_n by construction, so item 27 identifies S with the kernel complex. Conversely, a monomorphism of complexes is degreewise monic by item 31 and therefore identifies its source with a componentwise subobject stable under the differentials.

items.title: The first isomorphism theorem for complexes
items.strategy: Apply the published first isomorphism theorem in the ambient abelian category degreewise to f_n. Item 29 packages the component coimage-image isomorphisms into a chain isomorphism C/ker(f) isomorphic to im(f).

items.title: Finite biproducts of complexes are computed degreewise
items.strategy: The biproduct structure in item 30 is defined componentwise. Then the additivity of H_n from item 19 identifies the homology of a finite biproduct with the biproduct of the homology objects.

items.title: Products and coproducts of complexes are degreewise when they exist and preserve differentials
items.strategy: Whenever the ambient category admits the relevant products or coproducts of the terms, their universal properties assemble degreewise. The differential is the unique morphism induced by the component differentials, so the complex equation is checked componentwise.

items.title: An additive functor applies degreewise to complexes and chain maps
items.strategy: An additive functor preserves zero morphisms, so applying F to d_{n-1} d_n = 0 yields a new complex. The same componentwise application to a commuting square shows that F carries chain maps to chain maps.

items.title: An exact functor commutes with homology
items.strategy: Use exactness to identify F(Z_n C) with Z_n(F(C)) and F(B_n C) with B_n(F(C)) by preservation of kernels, images, and cokernels. The induced comparison from F(H_n C) to H_n(F(C)) is then the quotient isomorphism, and naturality comes from functoriality of the constructions.

items.title: An exact functor preserves quasi-isomorphisms and reflects them when it is conservative
items.strategy: Preservation follows by applying item 38 to the homology isomorphisms. If F is conservative and F(f) is a quasi-isomorphism, then item 38 identifies F(H_n(f)) as an isomorphism, so conservativity forces each H_n(f) to be an isomorphism.

items.title: Euler characteristic of a finite complex of finite-rank free abelian groups
Euler-Poincare formula for finite free complexes
items.strategy: Splice the short exact sequences 0 -> Z_n -> C_n -> B_{n-1} -> 0 and 0 -> B_n -> Z_n -> H_n -> 0, then use additivity of rank on short exact sequences and telescoping of the alternating sums.

items.title: FALSE: any sequence of morphisms is a chain complex
items.strategy: Refute the claim with two consecutive identity maps on a nonzero object; their composite is not zero, so the chain-complex axiom fails.

items.title: FALSE: the boundaries of a complex are a quotient of its cycles
items.strategy: Use the two-term complex 0 -> Z -> Q -> 0 in Ab: then Z_0 = Q and B_0 = Z, but every homomorphism Q -> Z is zero, so the boundary object is not a quotient of the cycle object.

items.title: FALSE: a chain map is determined by its maps on homology
items.strategy: Use the contractible two-term identity complex from the companion. Distinct chain maps can induce the same zero map on every homology object because all homology vanishes.

items.title: FALSE: every quasi-isomorphism is an isomorphism of complexes
items.strategy: The zero map from a nonzero acyclic complex to the zero complex induces isomorphisms on homology but is not invertible as a chain map.

items.title: FALSE: an additive functor commutes with homology
items.strategy: Item 38 shows exactness is the load-bearing hypothesis. A merely additive, nonexact functor can fail to preserve cycles, boundaries, or the quotient that defines homology.

items.title: FALSE: every infinite coproduct of complexes has homology equal to the coproduct of their homologies
items.strategy: Item 36 only constructs the degreewise coproduct complex when the coproducts exist. Without an AB4-type exactness hypothesis, taking homology need not commute with those infinite coproducts.

items.title: A zero-differential complex has homology equal to each term
items.strategy: Here Z_n(C) = C_n and B_n(C) = 0, so H_n(C) = C_n/0 is isomorphic to C_n in each degree.

items.title: A two-term complex has kernel and cokernel homology
items.strategy: For a two-term complex M -> N, H_1 is ker(f), H_0 is coker(f), and every other homology object is zero by direct computation of cycles and boundaries.

items.title: The multiplication-by-m complex computes a cyclic group
items.strategy: Apply the previous two-term computation to 0 -> Z -> Z -> 0 with differential multiplication by m. The kernel is 0 for m not equal to 0, and the cokernel is Z/mZ.

items.title: An exact short sequence as an acyclic three-term complex
items.strategy: View 0 -> A -> B -> C -> 0 as a three-term complex concentrated in degrees 2, 1, 0. Item 11 identifies the chain-complex exactness with the published exact-sequence notion, so all homology vanishes.

items.title: A split exact complex contracts degree by degree
items.strategy: Choose degreewise sections or retractions from the split short exact pieces and write the contracting homotopy explicitly on the three-term module complex. The example exhibits the formula without invoking the later general homotopy theory.

items.title: A chain map computed on cycles, boundaries, and homology
items.strategy: Pick a small complex of finitely generated abelian groups, compute Z_n and B_n in each degree, then evaluate the induced maps H_n(f) on the resulting quotients.

items.title: A quasi-isomorphism that is not an isomorphism of complexes
items.strategy: Include the zero complex into a contractible two-term identity complex. Both complexes have zero homology, so the map is a quasi-isomorphism, but it is not invertible on the underlying complexes.

items.title: Two distinct chain maps inducing the same homology map
items.strategy: Use two different endomorphisms of a contractible identity complex. Because every homology object is zero, both induced maps on homology agree even though the chain maps do not.

items.title: A subcomplex and its quotient complex
items.strategy: Take an explicit subcomplex of a finite module complex, compute the descended differential on the quotient degree by degree, and verify the formulas do not depend on the chosen representatives.

items.title: Euler-Poincare for a finite complex
items.strategy: Compute both alternating sums for a three-term free abelian-group complex and check they match as predicted by item 41.
